==English== ===Alternative forms=== * [[:bastid#English|bastid]] ([[Appendix:Glossary#pronunciation spelling|pronunciation spelling]]) ===Etymology===
    [[Category:English terms derived from Old French|BASTARD]][[Category:English terms derived from Middle English|BASTARD]][[Category:English terms derived from Latin|BASTARD]][[Category:English terms inherited from Middle English|BASTARD]][[Category:Pages with etymon|BASTARD]][[Category:English entries with etymon|BASTARD]][[Category:Pages using etymon with no ID|BASTARD]] [[File:Wyllelm bastard.jpg|right|thumb|220px|'ƿyllelm bastard' in the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, 1066]] From [[w:Middle English|Middle English]][[Category:English terms inherited from Middle English|BASTARD]][[Category:English terms derived from Middle English|BASTARD]] [[:bastard#Middle_English|bastard]], [[:bastarde#Middle_English|bastarde]], from [[w:Old English|Old English]][[Category:English terms inherited from Old English|BASTARD]][[Category:English terms derived from Old English|BASTARD]] [[:bastard#Old_English|bastard]] (used as an epithet), from [[w:Anglo-Norman language|Anglo-Norman]][[Category:English terms derived from Anglo-Norman|BASTARD]] [[:bastard#Old_French|bastard]], [[w:Old French|Old French]] [[:bastart#Old_French|bastart]] (“illegitimate child”), perhaps via [[w:Medieval Latin|Medieval Latin]][[Category:English terms derived from Medieval Latin|BASTARD]] [[:bastardus#Latin|bastardus]], of obscure[[Category:English terms with unknown etymologies|BASTARD]] origin. Likely from [[w:Frankish language|Frankish]][[Category:English terms derived from Frankish|BASTARD]] [[:Reconstruction:Proto-West Germanic/bāst|*bāst]] (“marriage, relationship”) + Old French [[:-ard#Old_French|-ard]], [[:-art#Old_French|-art]] (pejorative suffix denoting a specific quality or condition). Frankish ''*bāst'' derives from a [[w:North Sea Germanic|North Sea Germanic]] variety of [[w:Proto-Germanic language|Proto-Germanic]][[Category:English terms derived from Proto-Germanic|BASTARD]] [[:Reconstruction:Proto-Germanic/banstuz|*banstuz]] (“bond, connection, relationship, marriage with a second woman of lower status”), from [[w:Proto-Indo-European language|Proto-Indo-European]][[Category:English terms derived from Proto-Indo-European|BASTARD]] [[:Reconstruction:Proto-Indo-European/bʰendʰ-|*bʰendʰ-]] (“to tie, bind”) and is related to [[w:West Frisian language|West Frisian]] [[:boaste#West_Frisian|boaste]] (“marriage, matrimony”), [[w:Middle Dutch|Middle Dutch]] [[:bast#Middle_Dutch|bast]] (“lust, heat”), and more distantly to [[w:English language|English]] [[:boose#English|boose]] (“cow-stall”). The term probably originally referred to a child from a [[polygynous]] marriage of [[heathen]] Germanic custom — a practice not sanctioned by the Christian churches. Alternatively, and less likely, Old French ''bastart'' may have originated from the Old French term [[:fils de bast#Old_French|fils de bast]] (“[[packsaddle]] son”), meaning a child conceived on an improvised bed (medieval saddles often doubled as beds while travelling). However chronology makes this difficult, as ''bastard'' is attested in Old French from 1089 (Middle Latin ''bastardus'' as early as 1010), yet Old French ''bast'' (modern [[w:French language|French]] [[:bât#French|bât]]), though attested since 1130 with the meaning of "beast of burden", doesn't acquire the specific meaning of "packsaddle" until the 13c., making it too late to have given rise to the terms ''bastard'' and ''bastardus'' with this sense.
